result.summary: Pausanias describes the old statue of the pancratiast Arrhachion in Phigalia's market-place and tells how he won his last Olympic victory while dying. He then recalls the similar case of the boxer Creugas, killed by Damoxenus's foul blow at Nemea and crowned posthumously.

scenes.title: Arrhachion's statue at Phigalia
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the archaic stone statue of Arrhachion in the market-place, its inscription worn away.

scenes.title: Arrhachion's death and victory
scenes.summary: Arrhachion, in a deadly hold in the final bout, breaks his opponent's finger and dies; the opponent faints from pain and the Eleans crown the corpse.
scenes.stakes: Arrhachion is being strangled and will lose his life.

scenes.title: Creugas and Damoxenus at Nemea
scenes.summary: At dusk the boxers agree to exchange single blows; Damoxenus kills Creugas with a spear-hand strike, is expelled, and Creugas is awarded the victory and a statue at Argos.
scenes.stakes: Creugas risks his life trusting the agreement; Damoxenus risks disqualification by cheating.

characters.name: Arrhachion
characters.description: pancratiast of Phigalia, twice Olympic victor who won while dying

characters.name: Creugas
characters.description: boxer of Epidamnus killed at Nemea and awarded the crown

characters.name: Damoxenus
characters.description: Syracusan boxer who broke the agreement and killed Creugas

characters.name: Apollo
characters.description: god whose temple at Argos holds Creugas's statue

notable_quotes.reason: Vivid account of Arrhachion winning the contest in the moment of his own death.

analysis.text: The passage shows Greek athletic honour: fair play and the letter of agreements mattered, and a dead man could be declared victor.
The pancratium and early boxing were brutal sports, with limited protection, and umpires and judges enforced rules at the great festivals.

legacy.text: Arrhachion's death-victory became a famous anecdote of Greek athletics, retold by later writers such as Philostratus.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias dates Arrhachion's victories to the Olympiads before the 54th, around 564 BC, making him an early Olympic champion.

language_notes.text: Pancratiast: a competitor in the pancratium, an Olympic combat sport combining wrestling and boxing with very few rules.
Feet close together and arms at the sides describe the stiff, archaic style, like Egyptian-influenced early Greek figures.
Arrhachion won at two Olympiads before the 54th, so his victories were earlier, and the last was won posthumously. 'Equity of the umpires' means the judges' fairness.
Wild olive: the Olympic prize was a crown cut from a sacred wild olive tree.
Cestus: a boxing glove or strap of leather, later reinforced with metal. Here the thongs leave the fingers bare.
'Fingers straight out' is a spear-hand thrust. Damoxenus's sharpened nails made it lethal, so the blow broke the agreement.
Lycian Apollo: Apollo Lykeios, whose temple in Argos was a major sanctuary of the god as wolf-god or protector.

context_notes.text: Elis administered the Olympic Games, so its judges decided the victor, here awarding the crown posthumously.
Nemea was one of the four great Panhellenic games sites, and the Argives presided over its games.
Breaking agreed rules meant disqualification; Damoxenus was expelled and the dead man was declared victor.

literary_notes.text: The victor dies in the very moment of winning, while the apparent winner faints and loses; the reversal is the story's central paradox.
The graphic description of the blow and its effects makes Damoxenus's brutality and treachery vivid.
The short, blunt sentence after the gruesome detail makes the death seem sudden and final.
